title: Three toy supermarket chains, and the discounters behind them
lede: Toy supermarkets were a three-chain business for two decades. Lionel and Child World chased Toys “R” Us, tried to merge with each other twice, and closed within a year of each other.

blocks.title: Who won, who died
blocks.subtitle: The toy supermarket chains of the 1980s and what became of them.

items.name: Lionel (Kiddie City, Playworld)
items.text: Chapter 11 in 1982 and 1991. Liquidated from June 1993.[^16][^24]

items.name: Child World / Children’s Palace
items.text: The No. 2 chain. Filed for Chapter 11 on May 7, 1992 and ceased operations that summer after merger talks with Lionel failed.[^19][^21]

items.name: Toys “R” Us
items.text: The leader throughout. It outlived both rivals by 25 years, then closed its U.S. stores in 2018 under nearly $8 billion of debt.[^10][^32]

items.name: Kmart, Wal-Mart, Target
items.text: By 1993 the trade press said the spoils of the toy superstore contraction went to discounters with expanded toy departments.[^23]

blocks.body: Rankings moved around. The Times called Lionel the fourth largest toy chain in 1988 and the third largest chain of toy supermarkets in 1991.[^10][^16] The Morning Call in 1993 said it had been the second largest toy retailer.[^26] We report each claim with its source and do not pick one.
